newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers link Kevorkian to first AIDS suicide.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers link Kevorkian to first AIDS suicide.

text.p: Lawyers representing Dr. Jack Kevorkian confirmed Wednesday that a 27-year-old woman travelled to Michigan to commit suicide, the first AIDS patient ever to be linked to a man dubbed "Dr. Death."
Michael Schwartz, one of the attorneys representing Kevorkian, said Heidi Aseltyne of Indianapolis contracted the HIV virus while attending high school in Holt, Mich., near Lansing.

Aseltyne took her own life in a hotel room in the Detroit suburb of Romulus, said Schwartz. He refused to say if Kevorkian, the nation's most visible proponent of assisted suicide, was involved in her death.
"I cannot confirm whether or not she died as a result of anybody assisting her," Schwartz said at a news conference.

Aseltyne's family retained the law firm of Fieger, Fieger & Schwartz, which also represents Kevorkian, several days ago to shield them from "harrassment," Schwartz said. It was the fourth time since March that a person who came to Michigan to commit suicide has retained the firm.

At the news conference, Schwartz distributed copies of what he said was a genuine FBI facsimile cover sheet, accompanied by a memo discussing the possible "search/lockdown" of the law firm's offices in Southfield.
U.S. Attorney Saul Green and the FBI agent in charge of the Detroit office quickly released a statement denying that a search was planned, and calling the documents fake.

Schwartz claimed the firm received the sheets by fax Tuesday night. He said the FBI agent named on the form, Matt Iskrzycki, acknowledged the fax cover sheet was a legitimate FBI document, and some of the writing was his, but said otherwise the memo was a hoax.

Kevorkian has not admitted assisting in a suicide since last November, when he publicly acknowledged being present at his 45th death since 1990. But Michigan officials last week issued a "cease and desist" order warning the 68-year-old retired pathologist to stop practicing medicine without a license by helping people die.

He could face felony charges punishable by four years in jail and a $2,000 fine if found guilty of violating the order, which he burned publicly at a news conference April 4. His medical license was suspended in 1991 by the Michigan Department of Consumer and Industry Services.
Kevorkian is scheduled to go on trial in June in central Michigan for assisting in a suicide. He has been acquitted at three earlier trials on similar charges.

Physician-assisted suicide in the AIDS community is not unusual, said Stephen Jamison, an adjunct professor at the University of California at San Francisco, who has written on death and dying issues.

He said he knew of many AIDS patients who have contacted Kevorkian, but he theorised Kevorkian had not been active in helping them die because there is already a strong underground network in the AIDS community able to secure lethal drugs.
